title: Checkpoint: Extreme Objects and Other Worlds
objective: After this level you can compare the remnants stars leave behind and explain how we find other worlds.
summary: White dwarfs are Earth-sized, neutron stars city-sized, black holes have no surface. And thousands of other worlds await.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. From dead stars to living worlds.
cards.body: Level 70 said mass decides how a star ends. Here’s what each ending leaves behind, and how we learned to find things that barely want to be found.

cards.headline: What’s left when a star dies

items.label: Neutron star
points: About the size of a city

items.label: Black hole
points: Only an event horizon, the point of no return

cards.headline: Listening and looking
cards.body: Each discovery in this chapter came from reading a different signal. Pulsars give away neutron stars with radio beams that sweep past Earth like a lighthouse. Gravitational waves, first caught by LIGO in 2015, revealed two black holes merging. And tiny dips and wobbles in starlight have uncovered thousands of worlds around other stars, some, like TRAPPIST-1’s, in their habitable zones. Dead stars and new worlds, found the same way: by paying very close attention.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: What a dead star leaves behind, from a city-sized neutron star to a black hole nothing can escape.
Why a black hole doesn't suck everything in, and how an Earth-sized telescope captured one's image.
How astronomers find planets they can't see by watching the dips and wobbles of their stars.
Where life might exist beyond Earth, and what scientists look for in the air of faraway planets.

questions.prompt: Which stellar remnant is about the size of a city?

options.label: A red giant
options.rationale: Red giants are huge, living stars.

options.label: A black hole
options.rationale: Black holes aren’t measured that way.

questions.explanation: A neutron star crams more than the Sun’s mass into about 20 km.

questions.prompt: What instrument first detected gravitational waves?

options.label: The Event Horizon Telescope
options.rationale: The EHT imaged black holes in radio.

options.label: Voyager 1
options.rationale: Voyager explores the outer solar system.

questions.explanation: LIGO detected gravitational waves in 2015 from merging black holes.

questions.prompt: Why can’t a black hole itself be photographed directly?

options.label: It is too far away from Earth
It is hidden behind its planets
options.rationale: Black holes don’t hide behind planets.

options.label: It only exists in theory
options.rationale: Black holes have been imaged and detected.

options.label: No light escapes from inside its event horizon

questions.explanation: No light escapes from inside the event horizon, so there is no light from the black hole itself to photograph.

questions.prompt: A star dims by a tiny amount every 12 days. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A planet is transiting it on a 12-day orbit
The star is a pulsar
options.rationale: Pulsars pulse far faster, in radio.

options.label: The star is becoming a black hole

questions.explanation: A small, regular dip in a star’s light is the signature of a planet passing in front of it: a transit.

questions.prompt: Chapter 8 recap: which stellar remnant has no surface at all?

options.label: A white dwarf
options.rationale: It has a surface, about Earth’s size.

options.label: A pulsar
options.rationale: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star, with a surface.

options.label: A planetary nebula
options.rationale: That’s an expanding shell of gas, not a remnant core.

questions.explanation: White dwarfs and neutron stars have surfaces. A black hole has only an event horizon, the point of no return.
